patient.chief_complaint: Two-year history of worsening gait instability, urinary incontinence, and gradual cognitive decline
patient.history_present_illness: A 78-year-old retired schoolteacher with diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and bilateral knee osteoarthritis presented for inpatient NPH evaluation. Her daughter arranged the admission after noticing her mother's steady functional decline over the past two years. The patient initially attributed her walking difficulties to her knee arthritis, but her orthopedic surgeon noted that her gait pattern was atypical for osteoarthritis — short shuffling steps without significant knee pain during ambulation. She describes her feet as feeling 'stuck to the ground' when she tries to initiate walking. She has fallen four times in the past year, all without loss of consciousness. She now uses a rollator walker for all ambulation. Cognitive changes include increasing difficulty with finances — she accidentally paid the same bill three times in one month — and her daughter reports she repeats questions and has difficulty following complex television programs. She has been managing this independently but admits that she now struggles to follow her daughter's instructions for smartphone use. Urinary incontinence has been present for approximately 18 months; she wears protective pads daily and has stopped attending her church book club due to embarrassment. Her primary care physician obtained a head CT six months ago noting hydrocephalus and referred her for neurology evaluation. She was admitted for comprehensive NPH workup including MRI, lumbar puncture, and tap trial.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x3. MoCA 20/30. Impaired delayed recall (1/5), executive dysfunction on serial sevens and clock drawing. Processing speed reduced. No aphasia or agnosia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No papilledema. Horizontal and vertical gaze intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone. Mild symmetric hip flexor weakness (4+/5). No upper extremity weakness. No rigidity or tremor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Mild symmetric reduction in vibration sense at ankles bilaterally. Light touch and proprioception intact in hands and feet.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact. Heel-shin mildly clumsy bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Markedly apraxic with wide base, very short steps (step length approximately 15 cm), reduced foot clearance with shuffling. Freezing on initiation. TUG 32 seconds. 10-meter walk 26 seconds. Cannot tandem walk. Pull test positive — 3 steps back.
neurological_exam.additional: Bilateral grasp reflexes present. Snout reflex positive. No nuchal rigidity. Knee crepitus with range of motion but no effusions.

specialized_test.test_type: High-volume tap trial (42 mL) with quantitative gait assessment

findings.cognitive: MoCA improved from 20 to 23 (3 points at 24h)

specialized_test.impression: Positive tap trial. TUG improved 34% at 24 hours (32 sec to 21 sec); 10-meter walk improved 35% (26 sec to 17 sec); MoCA improved 3 points (20 to 23). Patient reported decreased urgency episodes at 24 hours

scores.assessment timing: immediately before the large-volume tap, then repeated after it

pre_post_comparison.before the tap: Markedly apraxic with wide base, very short steps (step length approximately 15 cm), reduced foot clearance with shuffling.; Freezing on initiation.; Pull test positive — 3 steps back.
pre_post_comparison.after the tap: Timed-up-and-go and 10-metre walk both improved, and the response meets the criterion this unit uses for a positive tap. This case does not record the percentages, so none is reported; the interpretation, not a fabricated number, is what the tap test yields here. The cognitive screen was repeated alongside

findings.result: Markedly apraxic with wide base, very short steps (step length approximately 15 cm), reduced foot clearance with shuffling.

clinical_assessment.impression: Objective gait and balance measured before the large-volume tap and repeated after it, with the cognitive screen repeated alongside. The response reached the threshold accepted as positive, which is the single best predictor of shunt response and the reason this measurement, not the imaging, carries the therapeutic decision. Without a measured baseline the post-tap change cannot be interpreted, which is why this assessment precedes the puncture.

output.impression: Markedly hyperdynamic aqueductal CSF flow. Peak velocity 24 cm/s (reference <18 cm/s); stroke volume 88 mcL/cycle (reference <42 mcL/cycle). Both values exceed published normative ranges
Negative — sparse-to-no amyloid neuritic plaque density. CL score 12, below the threshold of 24

Post-tap improvement in executive function and processing speed. Phonemic fluency (COWAT) improved from 6 to 10 words/min (67%). Processing speed improved from severely to moderately impaired. Memory (HVLT delayed recall) showed modest improvement from 3/12 to 4/12. The pattern of improvement is most pronounced in frontal-subcortical domains

findings.finding: Neurogenic detrusor overactivity — involuntary contractions at 120 mL, maximum capacity 200 mL. No evidence of bladder outlet obstruction or intrinsic sphincter deficiency.

output.impression: Neurogenic detrusor overactivity. Involuntary contractions at 120 mL; maximum cystometric capacity 200 mL. No outlet obstruction or intrinsic sphincter deficiency. Pattern is consistent with detrusor overactivity of neurogenic origin

findings.result: Reduced amplitude (4 mcV), borderline conduction velocity — mild distal axonal sensory neuropathy

output.impression: Mild distal axonal sensory neuropathy. Sural nerve sensory amplitude reduced at 4 mcV with borderline conduction velocity. Peroneal and tibial motor responses normal. Pattern is consistent with a length-dependent axonal sensory neuropathy

output.query: iNPH tap trial predictive value VP shunt outcomes older adults women

results.title: Gender differences in iNPH presentation and shunt outcomes
results.key_finding: Women with iNPH present slightly older and with more prominent incontinence; shunt outcomes equivalent to men when tap trial is clearly positive

results.title: Evans index and callosal angle as predictors of shunt response
results.key_finding: Evans index >0.38 and callosal angle <75° combined with positive tap trial yield >85% PPV for sustained VP shunt benefit

output.summary: Tap trial TUG improvement >20% combined with Evans index ≥0.38 and callosal angle <75° is associated with VP shunt benefit in iNPH (PPV >85%). In women with iNPH, shunt outcomes are equivalent to men when tap trial is clearly positive. Concurrent mild peripheral neuropathy does not appear to significantly impact gait outcomes following VP shunting in available series.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Small-vessel disease can produce gait apraxia and executive slowing, but ventriculomegaly out of proportion to white-matter burden and a positive tap test favour NPH
Shuffling gait overlaps, but absence of resting tremor, asymmetric rigidity, or L-dopa response and presence of magnetic gait + DESH favour NPH

Cognitive decline overlaps; AD typically presents with episodic-memory predominance and hippocampal atrophy rather than frontal-subcortical pattern and magnetic gait; CSF biomarkers / amyloid PET resolve copathology

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventriculomegaly proportionate to sulcal widening, callosal angle >90°, and absence of DESH or transependymal signal argue against true NPH
No history of trauma, SAH, or meningitis on review; would be considered if history suggested antecedent intracranial event

optimal_actions.action: Literature review of iNPH diagnostic criteria and shunt-response predictors
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Relkin 2005 INPH Study Group criteria; Tisell 2011 tap-test predictors; Williams 2016 review

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI — measure Evans index, callosal angle, assess DESH pattern; exclude mass effect, hydrocephalus from secondary cause, and atrophy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ventriculomegaly with Evans index >0.3, DESH pattern (tight high-convexity sulci + widened Sylvian fissures), callosal angle <90°, periventricular transependymal signal; no mass effect or aqueductal obstruction

optimal_actions.action: Reversible-cause labs (TSH, B12, RPR, HIV) to exclude metabolic / infectious dementia mimics
optimal_actions.expected_finding: TSH, B12, RPR, HIV negative or within normal range; reversible mimics excluded

optimal_actions.action: Baseline neuropsychological battery — subcortical/frontal pattern, and reference for pre/post-tap comparison
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Frontal-subcortical pattern: executive dysfunction and slowed processing predominate over episodic amnesia

optimal_actions.action: Large-volume lumbar puncture (30-50 mL tap test) with opening pressure and pre/post gait + neuropsych assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Opening pressure <25 cmH2O (normal); 30-50 mL CSF removed; pre/post tap gait and neuropsych assessment shows objective improvement supporting shunt-responsive iNPH

optimal_actions.action: Neurosurgery consultation for VP shunt candidacy and perioperative planning
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Neurosurgery accepts patient for VP shunt evaluation with programmable valve

optimal_actions.action: Amyloid PET (optional) — screen for AD copathology that may temper cognitive (but not gait) shunt benefit
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Inform shunt prognosis: AD copathology common (~50% iNPH)

optimal_actions.action: Measure gait and balance objectively before the large-volume tap — timed-up-and-go, 10-metre walk, step length, falls risk — and repeat the same measures and the cognitive screen after it. The baseline must be recorded before the puncture or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline timed gait recorded before the tap and repeated after it, with the response read against the >=20% threshold and the cognitive screen repeated alongside

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific for NPH and does not distinguish from neurodegenerative alternatives in this chronic gait/cognitive presentation
ECG is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of chronic gait + cognitive + urinary triad once cardiogenic syncope is not on the differential
Echocardiography does not contribute to NPH evaluation in the absence of syncope or cardioembolic stroke workup
Head CT is inferior to MRI for measuring Evans index and callosal angle and for excluding secondary causes; only justified if MRI is contraindicated
Cardiac monitoring has no diagnostic role in NPH and is reserved for syncope or arrhythmia workup

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede large-volume LP to exclude mass effect or secondary obstructive hydrocephalus before removing 30-50 mL of CSF
Baseline neuropsychological and gait assessment must be obtained before the tap test so that pre/post change can be measured (tap response is the shunt-response predictor)
The baseline gait and cognition must be measured before the large-volume tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted and the tap test yields nothing

critical_actions: Obtain brain MRI before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Document objective pre-tap gait (TUG and 10-metre walk) and neuropsychological baseline so that pre/post-tap change can be quantified
Remove 30-50 mL of CSF during the tap test (a low-volume LP under-samples and biases the test toward false negative)
Re-assess gait and cognition 1-4 hours after the tap and again at 24 hours (the response window for tap-test prediction of shunt benefit)
Refer to neurosurgery for VP shunt evaluation when imaging, clinical, and tap-test criteria support iNPH
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform large-volume lumbar puncture before MRI excludes mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Do not infer iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone — DESH, callosal angle <90°, and a clinical triad are required
Do not diagnose Alzheimer's disease in a patient with gait-predominant presentation and ventriculomegaly without first excluding NPH
Do not attribute the syndrome to 'normal ageing' or 'deconditioning' once the imaging criteria for ventriculomegaly are met
key_reasoning_points: iNPH diagnosis (Relkin 2005 INPH Study Group) requires (a) Hakim's triad of gait disturbance, cognitive impairment, and urinary urgency/incontinence — gait is typically first and most prominent; (b) ventriculomegaly with Evans >0.3 and DESH on MRI without mass effect; (c) age >40 and chronic course; (d) opening pressure <25 cmH2O; (e) absence of an alternative explanation
MRI is the imaging modality of choice — measure Evans index and callosal angle (<90° supports NPH) and confirm DESH (tight high-convexity sulci + wide Sylvian fissures)

The tap test is a 30-50 mL large-volume LP with pre/post objective gait (TUG, 10-metre walk) and neuropsychological assessment; opening pressure must be normal (<25 cmH2O) to satisfy the 'normal pressure' criterion
Tap-test sensitivity is only 50-80%; a single negative tap does not exclude NPH — an extended (3-5 day) lumbar drainage trial can resolve borderline cases
Reversible-cause labs (TSH, B12, RPR, HIV) are mandatory before attributing the syndrome to NPH
Approximately 50% of iNPH patients have AD copathology — this lowers cognitive benefit from shunting but does not negate gait benefit
Shunt response is best predicted by an objectively positive tap test or extended drainage trial in a patient who meets imaging and clinical criteria
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: The reversible-cause screen is good practice but does not establish or exclude hydrocephalus; the tap test does.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Gait ataxia is attributed to diabetic peripheral neuropathy
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Diabetic neuropathy produces sensory ataxia with reduced ankle vibration, not magnetic gait with freezing; ventriculomegaly + DESH indicate NPH
